Wastewater treatment via constructed wetlands (CWs) employs three (3) primary configurations: (1) free water surface (FWS, resembling natural marshes with exposed water), (2) horizontal subsurface flow (HSSF, water flows laterally through gravel substrate), and (3) vertical subsurface flow (VSSF, water percolates downward through layered media). Treatment mechanisms include biological processes (aerobic and anaerobic microbial degradation), physical processes (sedimentation, filtration), and chemical processes (adsorption, precipitation). Typical removal efficiencies are: BOD5 (biochemical oxygen demand) 80-95%, TSS (total suspended solids) 85-95%, TN (total nitrogen) 40-60%, and TP (total phosphorus) 30-50%. Hydraulic loading rates (HLR) for HSSF systems range from 2-5 cm/day. Design area requirements are approximately 5-10 m2 per population equivalent (PE). Plant species selection (commonly Phragmites australis, Typha spp., or Scirpus spp.) affects oxygen transfer to the rhizosphere and nutrient uptake capacity. Hybrid systems (combining VSSF and HSSF stages) achieve superior nitrogen removal (70-85%) through sequential nitrification-denitrification.
